papers.title: Effects of Active Learning-based Instructional Model in English Language Teaching for Thai Primary School Teachers
papers.abstract: This study aimed 1) to investigate the active learning activities commonly used in English language teaching of Thai primary school teachers, 2) to develop an instructional model based on active learning activities, 3) to implement the effectiveness of the instructional model based on the active learning activities with primary school teachers in Buriram Province, and 4) to evaluate the instructional model used. The participants in this study consisted of 30 Thai primary school teachers selected through volunteering technique in Lamplaimat District. The data were collected using a questionnaire, a handbook of communicative English skills related to active learning activities, lesson plans, the assessment of the capability in learning management based on active learning, communicative English tests, a satisfaction questionnaire, interviews, and the evaluation form of teaching and learning. The data were analyzed through frequency, mean, and standard deviation. The findings revealed that three active learning activities were recently developed: Games and Songs, Mind Mapping, and Role-Playing respectively. The active learning-based instructional model was designed to strengthen teachers’ English communication skills and to simultaneously evaluate teachers’ instructional skills. Most importantly, teachers who were trained through these active learning models showed significant improvement in their English communication abilities. Their average post-test scores were significantly higher than their pre-test scores at the .01 level. The study concluded that the active learning-based instructional model can effectively enhance English language teaching skills among primary school teachers, and beneficially provide a practical framework for teacher training and educational development in Buriram Province with similar educational contexts.

papers.title: Understanding how learning through play works: a path analysis of school supports, classroom quality and child holistic learning in crisis-affected schools in Ethiopia
papers.abstract: Introduction Learning through play (LtP) has emerged as a promising approach for supporting children's holistic learning and development in conflict and crisis-affected settings. While emerging evidence suggests that LtP can improve children's academic, social-emotional, wellbeing, and creative outcomes, less is known about the mechanisms through which these outcomes are achieved. This study examines pathways linking school-level supports, teacher-level processes, and child-level outcomes within PlayMatters, a large-scale LtP intervention implemented in refugee and host-community schools in Ethiopia. Methods We used cross-sectional endline data collected as part of a randomized controlled trial conducted in 35 primary schools assigned to treatment and control groups, including 252 teachers and 2,755 students. We estimated a multilevel path analysis examining relationships between school-level implementation supports (supportive administration, peer collaboration, and availability of teaching and learning materials), teacher-level processes (attitudes and beliefs toward LtP, instructional quality, and teacher-student relationships), and children's literacy, numeracy, empathy, and wellbeing outcomes. Results Academic and social-emotional outcomes appeared to operate through partially different pathways. Academic outcomes were more closely associated with instructional quality emphasizing active learning, whereas empathy and wellbeing were more closely associated with teacher-student relationships. Although supportive administration and the availability of hands-on learning materials were associated with more positive attitudes toward LtP, these attitudes did not independently predict observed instructional quality, suggesting that positive beliefs alone may be insufficient to change classroom practice. Discussion The findings suggest that LtP may contribute to different domains of child development through distinct instructional and relational pathways. They underscore the importance of strengthening the institutional and professional supports that enable teachers to translate positive attitudes toward LtP into effective classroom practices in crisis-affected schools.

papers.title: X-ray microtomography and automated classification methods to quantify recycling effects on a modified AA7050 additive manufacturing alloy
papers.abstract: Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) offers near-net shaping and lower per-part costs compared to casting. Lower costs depend partly on the recyclability of LPBF feedstock powder, which is only selectively melted and can be recollected and reused. As particles are spattered, condensed, or segregated by laser heat, it is essential that reliable sieving and mixing methods are used to maintain consistent feedstock characteristics. The effects of printing, sieving, and mixing on aluminum alloy feedstock powder were characterized by three-dimensional (3D) x-ray microscopy, which was used to classify individual particles in repeatedly recycled powder. Contrary to previous recycling studies using 2D microscopy and sieve analysis to measure powder populations, a tomography-based approach showed a decrease in median particle diameter after each recycling step. By examining classified particles, we found that elongated and flattened particles with dimensions above the sieve size were retained in the virgin condition then gradually removed by repeated recycling. The tomography analysis is presented, alongside electron microscopy characterization of elemental segregation, to thoroughly describe the recyclability of a unique AM alloy and demonstrate the interpretability of tomography-based powder analysis in the context of powder metallurgy.

papers.title: Bayesian hierarchical uncertainty quantification of a helical-path tortuosity predictor for modeling hydraulic conductivity in sandstone aquifers
papers.abstract: Hydraulic conductivity and effective diffusivity in saturated sandstone aquifers depend on the square of tortuosity, so using a point estimate of tortuosity leaves its contribution to uncertainty unquantified in groundwater-flow and contaminant-transport models. A Bayesian hierarchical framework quantifies uncertainty in a published helical-path tortuosity predictor using a dataset of 51 sandstone samples spanning three formation classes: Tight German sandstones, clean Fontainebleau-analogous sandstones, and unconsolidated high-connectivity sandstones. The framework propagates uncertainty to hydrogeological quantities using the existing model and published data. Posterior predictions of tortuosity agree with the observations, with a mean absolute percentage error of approximately 3.3% and conservatively calibrated predictive intervals. Convergence was assessed using rank-normalized split $$\widehat{R}$$ R ^ , effective sample sizes, and autocorrelation times, and out-of-sample performance was assessed using Pareto-smoothed importance-sampling leave-one-out and five-fold cross-validation (held-out mean absolute percentage error near 5.1%). Fixing the class critical porosities at their published values and inferring them yield statistically indistinguishable predictions, with information-criterion differences within two paired standard errors; the comparison is a robustness check, and the published thresholds remain within the credible intervals under widened and flat priors, although the data constrain them mainly from above. The tortuosity posterior is then propagated into the formation factor, the effective diffusivity and a multiplicative hydraulic-conductivity uncertainty factor, and an ensemble of one-dimensional transport simulations converts these into 90% envelopes on contaminant plume extent and on diffusive breakthrough time through a low-permeability layer, providing uncertainty bounds for models of the sandstone classes studied.

papers.title: A comprehensive review and unified taxonomy of intelligent hybrid fractional-order models incorporated with machine learning in healthcare applications
papers.abstract: Fractional-order differential equations (FDEs) describe memory and hereditary effects that integer-order models cannot capture, while machine-learning (ML) methods extract patterns from large and noisy clinical data but often lack mechanistic meaning. Combining the two has become an active research direction in healthcare, yet the literature is spread across many disease areas and there is no common way to describe how the coupling is actually implemented. This review addresses that gap. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed and OpenAlex for journal articles published between January 2018 and March 2026 and used Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for citation searching. After screening 209 records, 43 hybrid FDE–ML studies were included. We propose a two-level taxonomy in which three coupling types (ML-informed estimation of fractional parameters; fractional physics-informed neural networks (FPINNs) and neural solvers; and fractional preprocessing of features) describe the mathematical link, and a fourth type describes the deployment layer (simulation engine and clinician-facing interface). We define a hybrid operator Q with an explicit domain and range that expresses every reviewed model as a composition of these components, and we illustrate it on the public UCI Dermatology dataset using repeated stratified cross-validation, baseline classifiers, and bootstrap confidence intervals. The evidence tables show that FPINNs and neural solvers dominate infectious-disease modelling, whereas oncology and cardiometabolic studies more often combine several types. Reported gains are study-specific, so we present them as representative values rather than pooled effects. We also discuss computational cost, data scarcity, uncertainty quantification, regulatory validation, and fairness. The main contribution of the work is a reproducible classification and a formal operator that can guide model selection, reporting, and validation in future hybrid fractional–ML studies in healthcare.

papers.title: BECF: A Unified Cross-Layer Risk Scoring Framework for Healthcare IoT Security with Blockchain Anomaly Detection and Explainable Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: Healthcare Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) security and blockchain consent governance remain siloed: intrusion detection systems monitor network traffic but ignore blockchain transaction anomalies, while blockchain anomaly detectors largely target general financial contexts. We propose the Blockchain-Enabled Cybersecurity Framework (BECF), a benchmark-validated architectural proof-of-concept that integrates temporally validated, SHAP-explainable gradient boosting for intrusion detection on ToN-IoT, probability-calibrated blockchain anomaly detection on Elliptic, smart-contract consent management on Ethereum Sepolia, and a composite risk function fusing network intrusion probability, blockchain anomaly probability, and patient data sensitivity. Fusion weights and classifiers are optimized through constrained grid search and Bayesian optimization, with bootstrap confidence intervals and controlled post-hoc comparisons. On ToN-IoT, the Bayesian-optimized LightGBM classifier achieves 99.89% accuracy (95% CI: [99.85%, 99.92%]), F1 = 0.9993, and MCC = 0.9969; on Elliptic, LightGBM achieves 76.63% balanced accuracy, F1 = 0.6290, and AUPRC = 0.5854 for general illicit Bitcoin transaction detection—not healthcare-consent attack detection. Smart contracts achieve 99.8% success, zero critical findings from the applied analyzers, and approximately 17.8% gas savings. Across 10,000 controlled integration-test events, BECF achieves a 74.4% event-level true positive rate for dual-layer alerts with a false-positive rate of 0.20%, and detects all 47 explicitly constructed coordinated scenarios (47/47; 100%; 95% Wilson CI: [92.4%, 100%]). These scenarios were generated in a controlled integration testbed and do not represent naturally occurring clinical attacks; therefore, the scenario result is controlled feasibility evidence rather than clinical detection performance. Prospective hospital validation and Ethereum-native attack validation remain necessary before clinical deployment.

papers.abstract: This study identified, characterized, and classified GeoGebra-mediated teaching strategies in university mathematics education through a scoping review of empirical research published between 2015 and 2026. The review followed Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting recommendations. Searches were conducted in Google Scholar in Spanish and English on October 19 and 21, 2026, respectively. Of 56 documents examined, 25 were selected for descriptive and narrative synthesis. The studies were organized into five analytical groupings: problem-solving and mathematical modeling (28%), guided inquiry and exploration (12%), collaborative learning and active learning approaches (16%), instructional sequences focused on conceptual understanding (28%), and initial teacher education (16%). GeoGebra supported dynamic visualization, coordination of mathematical representations, and exploration of mathematical relationships. The findings indicate that using GeoGebra does not, in itself, constitute a teaching strategy; its educational role depends on the mathematical tasks, pedagogical approaches, and organization of learning activities.

papers.title: INTEGRATING DIGITAL PEDAGOGICAL TOOLS AND INCLUSIVE TEACHING PRACTICES: IMPLICATIONS FOR LEARNING STRATEGIES AND PROFESSIONAL ETHICS AMONG B.ED. SCIENCE STUDENTS UNDER NEP 2020
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital educational technologies has transformed the possibilities for science teaching, inclusive learning, and professional development. However, meaningful integration requires more than access to digital resources; it requires pedagogical judgment, sensitivity to learner diversity, effective learning strategies, and ethical responsibility. This thematic paper examines the integration of digital pedagogical tools and inclusive teaching practices in B.Ed. science teacher education in the context of India’s National Education Policy (NEP) 2020. Drawing on recent literature, international competency frameworks, inclusive education principles, and Indian educational policy, the paper develops five interconnected themes: purposeful digital pedagogy, inclusive science lesson design, learner-centred strategies, professional ethics in technology use, and institutional support for responsible digital transformation. It proposes an original conceptual framework, the Inclusive Digital Science Pedagogy and Ethics (IDSPE) Framework, which connects technology selection, accessibility, active learning, ethical decision-making, and reflective professional practice. The paper argues that digital tools can support differentiated instruction, scientific visualization, collaborative inquiry, and formative assessment when they are selected according to educational purpose and learner needs. At the same time, inaccessible platforms, digital inequality, inaccurate AI-generated content, privacy risks, and overdependence on automated systems may undermine inclusive educational goals. The paper recommends integrating digital competence, universal design, responsible AI literacy, and reflective ethical practice into B.Ed. science curricula. It concludes that the success of educational technology under NEP 2020 should be judged not by the quantity of tools used but by their contribution to equitable participation, meaningful scientific understanding, and responsible professional practice.

papers.title: Two-stage attention-guided active learning for nonstationary Gaussian process modeling in robust parameter design
papers.abstract: Robust parameter design is vital for continuous quality improvement in industrial practice. However, modeling nonstationary response surfaces with limited data remains challenging because insufficient predictive accuracy may introduce optimistic bias in estimating optimal parameter settings. We propose a two-stage attention-inspired active learning method within a nonstationary Gaussian process (NSGP) modeling framework for robust parameter design. This two-stage acquisition first ranks candidates by expected quality loss and then applies a maximin rule to preserve subset diversity. In the first stage, candidate design points are ranked by their relevance to the specified target region, and a subset with high relevance scores is selected for further refinement. In the second stage, spatial diversity is enforced by selecting additional points from this subset to mitigate clustering. The selected points are used to update the training set and NSGP model. A genetic algorithm solves the NSGP-based robust parameter design problem and determines optimal settings. Comparisons with classical design baselines and three modern acquisition criteria show that the proposed method improves predictive accuracy and enhances the robustness of solutions under limited data. The effectiveness of the method is further supported by ablation experiments, target-value sensitivity analysis, and a modified 10-variable Wing Weight analytical benchmark.

papers.title: A Unified Ornstein–Uhlenbeck–Lévy–Branching Framework for Interpretable Modeling of Cancer Evolution
papers.abstract: Biological evolution arises from the interplay of continuous stochastic dynamics, discontinuous transitions, branching-associated diversification, environmental perturbations, and imperfect experimental observations. Existing stochastic models—including Brownian motion, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) processes, Lévy jump processes, and branching processes—capture complementary aspects of these dynamics but have largely been developed as separate methodological frameworks. We present the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck–Lévy–Branching (OULB) framework, a unified probabilistic model for multiscale biological evolution that integrates continuous dynamics, discontinuous jumps, branch-associated regime dynamics, therapy-dependent attractor shifts, and observation models within a common latent-state representation. Brownian motion provides an unconstrained diffusion baseline, while classical OU, treatment-shifted OU, OU–Lévy, and OU–Branching models arise as nested or constrained formulations within the broader framework. Using a comprehensive simulation platform, we demonstrate generally reliable recovery of continuous stochastic parameters, condition-dependent recovery of jump events and branch-associated regime structure, and improved parameter estimation under sparse, noisy, and irregularly sampled observations. Independent predictive model comparison further delineates the conditions under which candidate dynamical mechanisms can be distinguished and shows reduced discrimination with sparse sampling, increased measurement noise, temporal confounding, and model misspecification. We further introduce an empirical calibration strategy that derives simulation settings from longitudinal cancer evolution data, enabling biologically grounded methodological evaluation. A modular computational workflow integrates simulation, Bayesian inference, calibration, visualization, and uncertainty quantification. The OULB framework establishes a unified mathematical and computational foundation for interpretable, extensible, and reproducible probabilistic modeling across longitudinal, spatial, and multimodal biological systems.

papers.title: Weak-strong uniqueness for the coupled Maxwell and inertial Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equations
papers.abstract: The coupled Maxwell and inertial Landau--Lifshitz--Gilbert equations are considered with initial data and inhomogeneity supported in a bounded domain. In the interior domain, the time-dependent inertial Landau--Lifshitz--Gilbert equation is coupled with Maxwell interior equations and Maxwell boundary integral equations. We prove that if a strong solution of the coupled system exists for some time interval, it must coincide with every weak solution on that interval. In contrast to earlier results, the present analysis incorporates inertial effects and the coupling with the space-dependent form of Maxwell boundary integral equations. Moreover, our proof accounts for all physically relevant lower-order terms appearing in the inertial Landau--Lifshitz--Gilbert equation, including an applied field, uniaxial anisotropy, a stray field, and the Dzyaloshinskii--Moriya interaction. We present an illustrative physics-informed neural network experiment whose training histories and computed field distributions complement the uniqueness result.

papers.title: Slack-based stochastic Model Predictive Control
papers.abstract: This article introduces a Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework that leverages a pair of complementary slack variables to quantify constraint violation and robustness, enabling linear probabilistic constraint enforcement. Central to this approach is the definition of an interpretable slack ratio that serves as a monotonic proxy for the violation probability under a mild stochastic-ordering assumption that admits decision-dependent dispersion of the constraint margin, beyond additive-disturbance settings. For location–scale distributions (e.g., Gaussian, Uniform, Laplace), this ratio is invariant to the disturbance mean and variance for a fixed violation probability. We exploit this property to pre-compute low-complexity safety margins that guarantee constraint satisfaction with high confidence at the first prediction step—and along the whole horizon for disturbance families closed under convolution, e.g., the Gaussian case—eliminating the need for online variance estimation. Simulation results demonstrate the applicability of the proposed method in practical problems.

papers.title: Physiological digital twins require cross-system observation contracts
papers.abstract: Whole-body models explain how organ systems can be represented and coupled. A model that is updated repeatedly from patient measurements must also specify when those measurements support a particular conclusion. This Hypothesis and Theory article proposes an Observation Contract Framework: a declared set of evidence requirements for each output, checked whenever that output is requested. Each system uses 10 fields covering target states, direct measurements, proxies, unmeasured states, events, reference measurements, timing, quality failures, prohibited conclusions and measurement readiness. The framework returns permit, degrade or block for each output. Five testable hypotheses address unsupported conclusions, timing errors, missing reference measurements, cross-system dependencies and the distinction between signal reconstruction and state validation. The framework is specified for eight peripheral systems, with central nervous system dependencies explicitly left unobserved. A mathematical oxygen-delivery example explains how system requirements are combined. A small retrospective replay of public critical-care records then illustrates the same rules: a record-based oxygen-delivery proxy can be restricted or withheld as haemoglobin measurements become outdated, while a validated physiological oxygen-delivery claim remains blocked. This replay is an application example, not a clinical validation or a comparative test of the hypotheses. Existing sensors support many bounded measurements, but do not continuously identify regional perfusion, venous capacitance, ventilation–perfusion mismatch, endocrine pulsatility, tissue immune activity or in vivo coagulation potential. The framework complements context-of-use definition, observability and identifiability analysis, model interoperability, verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification. Its purpose is to state what evidence is needed for a conclusion and what must be withheld when that evidence is insufficient.

papers.title: Peer Instruction in Hybrid Computing Courses: The Relationships Between Student Modality, Discussion, and Learning
papers.abstract: Background: Peer instruction is an active learning pedagogy that emphasizes collaboration and learning from one’s peers. Prior research in computing education has shown that using peer instruction can improve students’ learning, reduce dropout and failure rates, and result in larger increases in students’ self-efficacy relative to standard lecture-based instruction. However, it has not investigated the use of peer instruction in hybrid courses, which have become increasingly popular in higher education due to their flexibility and ability to manage increases in enrollment. Objectives: We evaluated the effectiveness of peer instruction at facilitating students’ learning of computing concepts in in-person and online modalities of a hybrid course. Additionally, we examined how students’ discussions between rounds of peer instruction relate to their learning of computing concepts and whether these relationships vary when courses follow different attendance policies. Context and Methods: We analyzed students’ normalized learning gains from peer instruction in two offerings of a hybrid undergraduate data science course where students could choose to attend class meetings in person or synchronously online. In the first (open-policy) offering, students could self-select their modality for each class meeting and alternate modalities at will. In the second (closed-policy) offering, students needed to obtain instructor permission each time they wanted to attend class online, which drastically reduced the proportion of students who did so. Findings: Students who attended class online in the open-policy offering experienced smaller normalized learning gains than students who attended class in person in either offering. Additionally, in the open-policy offering, students who discussed the peer instruction questions in person experienced higher normalized learning gains than students who engaged in discussion online. Lastly, students who engaged in in-person discussion in the open-policy offering experienced higher normalized learning gains than students who did so in the closed-policy offering. Implications: Our results suggest that peer instruction may be more effective in person as opposed to online, particularly if there are differences in discussion environments across modalities. Additionally, they provide insight into how students’ discussion behaviors are related to their modalities. We encourage other instructors to take them into consideration when designing and implementing peer instruction in a hybrid computing course.

papers.title: Fault Diagnosis of Reciprocating Compressor Crosshead Nut Loosening Using Swin Transformer-Based Ordered Transfer Learning
papers.abstract: The connecting nut between the piston rod and the crosshead is a key fastener of reciprocating compressors, and its loosening may lead to unplanned shutdowns and even safety accidents. Fault severities are commonly divided into normal, slight, moderate and severe states, but accurate data-driven diagnosis under variable working conditions remains difficult because labeled experimental fault data are scarce and the fault features of different severities are separated in scale. This paper proposes the Swin Transformer Deep Ordered Transfer Network with Multi-Scale Feature Fusion, CORAL Alignment and Ordinal Regression (Swin-MCO). The source domain is a rigid-flexible coupled multibody simulation validated against bench measurements, and the target domain is a test-bench dataset covering 25 speed and pressure conditions, of which only 20% are labeled for training. The model extracts hierarchical features from 224 × 224 angular-domain texture images, aligns second-order statistics across domains and encodes the physical fault progression in the classifier. The diagnosis accuracies reach 95.80%, 95.57% and 96.72% on the three unseen test sets, and misclassifications are confined to adjacent severity levels. The results indicate that the proposed model provides an effective solution for cross-domain diagnosis of connecting nut loosening. Future work will focus on industrial deployment, lightweight edge implementation and uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: Mapping Middens: Multimodal Imagery Illuminates Rhino Space Use in Savanna Landscapes
papers.abstract: Ecosystem engineering by many animal species creates distinct features across landscapes that shape biodiversity and ecosystem structure and serve as key signatures of animal space use. Remote sensing has been used to map the spatial distributions of such features across landscapes, enhancing our ability to characterize the biotic factors that create resource heterogeneity. However, some animal‐engineered features are challenging to reliably detect even with high‐resolution remotely sensed imagery, limiting our understanding of how ecosystem engineering shapes ecological processes and animal spatial behavior. In African savannas, communal dung middens created by rhinos are central to olfactory communication and nutrient redistribution, but their spatial distribution and the environmental factors shaping midden placement have not been quantified. We used coincident high‐resolution thermal, RGB, and LiDAR data to detect and map rhino middens in Kruger National Park, South Africa, and demonstrate that active learning using multimodal imagery can efficiently detect middens across large areas. We then analyzed midden spatial patterning and used remotely sensed habitat metrics to quantify drivers of midden placement across spatial scales. Although we found weak and inconsistent deviations from complete spatial randomness in midden spatial patterning, midden placement was not random but strongly associated with proximity to or density of animal paths, proximity to water, and low levels of vegetation cover. These midden sites likely offer ease of access in areas of high rhino traffic that further facilitates the broadcasting of social cues. We found no relationship between midden placement and terrain attributes, suggesting that middens are placed throughout the topographic landscape, providing new insights into rhino space use. We demonstrate how using multimodal remote sensing data can facilitate a scalable approach to detecting cryptic animal‐made features in heterogeneous landscapes, providing a foundation for studying broad‐scale impacts of overlooked ecosystem engineering features that can be used to inform conservation strategy.

papers.title: Motion planning and control integrated with LLM for unstructured terrain with slope restrictions
papers.abstract: To address the core challenges of autonomous driving motion planning in complex unstructured environments, this paper proposes an integrated solution that combines slope constraints, large language model parameter optimization, and large language model obstacle avoidance decision-making. First, a slope-aware 3D Hybrid A* path planning algorithm with a multi-objective cost function and an optimized heuristic function is proposed. Secondly, an adaptive parameter optimization framework integrating Hybrid A* with Large Language Model (LLM) is developed, dynamically adjusting key parameters through a closed-loop mechanism. Finally, an LLM-assisted model predictive control (MPC) scheme for trajectory tracking and obstacle avoidance is developed, which achieves a balanced trade-off between tracking accuracy and collision safety. The proposed obstacle avoidance method is compared with alternative approaches.

papers.title: PHYSICS-INFORMED NEURAL NETWORK-BASED SENSORLESS SPEED ESTIMATION OF BRUSHLESS DIRECT CURRENT MOTOR DRIVE
papers.abstract: Brushless direct current (BLDC) motors are employed for electric vehicles (EVs), medical equipment, and military robots because of their fast dynamic speed response and wide range of speed regulation characteristics. However, conventional methods are not suitable for dynamic speed-varying conditions, which leads to parameter variation issues and longer computational time. Therefore, in this article, a novel Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for sensorless speed detection of a BLDC motor is implemented using a machine learning-based physics-informed neural network (PINN) algorithm. Variables obtained from the PINN training are incorporated into the novel EKF; then, with the implemented model, the BLDC motor speed tracks the reference speed in dynamic, speed-varying conditions, thereby eliminating parameter variation issues and achieving shorter computational time as well. The implemented sensorless speed estimation scheme is compared with the conventional algorithms, and the results are presented using LAUNCHXL-F28379D. Also, compared with other conventional sensorless speed estimation techniques, the implemented method achieved reduced speed errors of 0.003% and 0.03% at 1500 rpm and 2000 rpm, respectively.

papers.title: Medial Malleolar Cortical Thickening with Non metallic implants for Prophylactic fixation in Total Ankle Arthroplasty.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Metal and non-metal fixation has long been utilized in orthopedic procedures but carries drawbacks including migration, breakage, osteolysis, imaging interference, and potential need for removal. Although absorbable hardware has historically shown mixed results, advancements in bio-integrative technology promise non-metal alternatives that reduce stress shielding and support healing. Periprosthetic fracturing in the setting of total ankle arthroplasty (TAA) is an area of high concern which can lead to severe clinical ramifications. PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to assess changes in medial malleolar thickness in TAA specifically comparing use of integrative technology to a control. STUDY DESIGN/METHODS: The authors reviewed a single surgeon operative database of patients who underwent primary total ankle replacement (TAR) between December 2018 and February 2024 with a minimum of 1 year follow up. Ninety-one subjects that underwent TAA were included in this study. RESULTS: We found a statistically significant increase in cortical thickness post-operatively in the group who had prophylactic fixation of the medial malleolus with the bio-integrative implant compared to preoperative cortical thickness, with an average increase of 0.63 cm (p-value < 0.0001). However, this finding did not demonstrate an association with the incidence of medial malleolar stress fractures. CONCLUSION: Although biointegrative prophylactic fixation was associated with increased medial malleolar cortical thickness following TAA, the clinical significance of this finding remains uncertain. Further studies are warranted to determine whether biointegrative fixation provides meaningful protection against medial malleolar stress fractures. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3, retrospective cohort study.

papers.title: Transcriptomic Characterization of Early Osseointegration: An Exploratory In Vivo RNA-Seq Study.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: This exploratory in vivo RNA-seq study investigated early molecular responses at the bone-implant interface of commercially available titanium (Ti) dental implants using a rabbit tibia model at 10 days post-implantation. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Three screw-shaped (4.0 mm × 8.0 mm) implant types were prepared: (1) turned Ti, (2) SLA-modified Ti, and (3) turned copper (Cu). Four sites-including a drilled Sham control-were placed in the tibiae of four New Zealand white rabbits. Surface roughness parameters and chemical composition were evaluated (n = 3). Histomorphometric analysis was performed to assess bone-to-implant contact (BIC) and bone area (BA). Peri-implant tissue was harvested for RNA extraction and sequenced using the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform. Transcriptome-wide differential gene expression analysis was performed, followed by gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis. Multiple-testing correction was performed using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) method. RESULTS: Both Ti groups yielded significantly higher BIC and BA than Cu (P < .001). Transcriptome-wide analysis identified 28 differentially expressed genes (FDR-adjusted P < .05, log₂(fold change) > 1 or < -1), which clustered into three functional categories: pro-inflammatory mediators, immunoregulatory/innate defense responses, and mitochondrial/stress-related pathways. SLA Ti showed a transcriptional pattern suggestive of coordinated immune-related signaling (increased expression of TNF, IL 1α, Gal-3, ORM1, and S100A6), whereas turned Cu exhibited upregulation of mitochondrial and oxidative stress-related genes alongside reduced antioxidant and innate defense markers. Notably, no genes met the differential expression criteria in the SLA Ti versus turned Ti comparison. CONCLUSIONS: This exploratory RNA-seq study identified distinct transcriptional profiles during early peri-implant healing. The findings provide preliminary insight into molecular events occurring at the bone-implant interface and may serve as a foundation for future studies investigating the biology of osseointegration.

papers.title: Seventeen-Year Follow-up of Migrated Dental Implants with a Prosthesis: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Long-term migration of osseointegrated dental implants is a rare clinical phenomenon. This case report describes a 17-year follow-up of a patient who experienced implant migration more than a decade after functional loading. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A 58-year-old female patient with advanced periodontal disease underwent comprehensive implant therapy. Following full-mouth extractions except for teeth 34 and 43, six implants were placed in the maxilla and six in the mandible. A maxillary cross-arch implant-supported fixed partial denture (IS-FPD) and three mandibular IS-FPDs (at sites 36-35, 33-42, and 44-46) were delivered. After 12 years of stable function, migration of implants at sites 33 and 42, along with adjacent teeth 34 and 43 and their prosthesis, was identified. Following the extraction of the adjacent natural teeth, a new mandibular cross-arch prosthesis was fabricated over the existing, stable implants. RESULTS: Despite the multi-directional migration, the migrated implants maintained the stability without any mechanical or structural failure. The patient was monitored for an additional 5 years (17 years of total follow-up), during which the implants remained stable in their new clinical positions without further complications. CONCLUSIONS: Re-prosthetic intervention can achieve long-term functional stability for migrated dental implants. Non-surgical prosthetic approach implies an optional treatment strategy for managing long-term implant migration while preserving the function under the clinical and radiographic stability compatible with osseointegration.

papers.title: Effects of Cover Screw and Healing Abutment on Early Implant Stability: A Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: This randomized split-mouth controlled clinical trial compared the effects of a cover screw and a healing abutment on implant stability during early osseointegration. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Systemically healthy individuals requiring at least two dental implants were included in this split-mouth study; one implant received a healing abutment (one-stage protocol) and the contralateral implant a cover screw (two-stage protocol). Treatment allocation was randomized using sealed opaque envelopes. Primary implant stability was assessed by insertion torque and resonance frequency analysis. Implant Stability Quotient (ISQ) values were recorded at baseline and at 3-month follow-up, and changes in implant stability (ΔISQ) were analysed. The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07687615). RESULTS: The study included 46 systemically healthy individuals. No significant differences were observed between the groups with respect to baseline ISQ values or insertion torque (p>0.05). However, both the 3-month ISQ values and ΔISQ were significantly greater in the cover screw group than in the healing abutment group (p<0.05). The mean 3-month ISQ value was 77.77±3.14 in the cover screw group and 75.63±5.03 in the healing abutment group (p=0.001). Baseline insertion torque was positively correlated with the 3-month ISQ values in both protocols (p<0.001). CONCLUSION: Submerged healing with a cover screw resulted in a modest but statistically significant increase in the secondary implant stability. However, because the absolute inter-group difference was small and both groups achieved mean ISQ values above 70, no clinically significant advantage of either protocol was detected during the 3-month follow-up period.

papers.title: Design and PINN-Kriging assisted multi-objective optimization of a dual-electrical-port in-wheel motor for HEV electromagnetic E-CVT
papers.abstract: Direct-drive in-wheel motors (IWMs) are constrained by low torque density and the unsprung mass penalty associated with size scaling, while geared reductions suffer from inherent gear clearance and NVH degradation. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a hybrid-flux dual-electrical-port in-wheel motor (DEP-IWM) designed for electromagnetic electro-stepless transmission (E-CVT) in hybrid electric vehicles. Featuring a coaxial single-stator dual-rotor topology with twin independent windings, the proposed motor achieves seamless electromagnetic power split without mechanical planetary gear sets. The outer rotor employs a tangential flux-concentrating array that functions dual-purpose as a “dynamic magnetic bridge” and a flux-modulation structure. Concurrently, the inner rotor incorporates an eccentric pole-scraping geometry, which effectively eliminates high-order air-gap harmonics while avoiding the manufacturing complexity of Halbach arrays. To address the multi-parameter, strongly coupled optimization inherent to dual-port topologies, a physics-informed surrogate model combining Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Kriging (PINN-Kriging) was constructed by embedding Maxwell partial differential equations into the loss function, followed by multi-objective inverse optimization via NSGA-II algorithm combined with engineering-preference TOPSIS decision-making. Finite element verification demonstrates that the optimized outer-rotor torque density increases by 192.5% compared with conventional dual-drive counterparts, while torque ripples for the outer and inner rotors are suppressed to 4.45% and 3.77%, respectively. This study offers a high-efficiency, ripple-suppression direct-drive solution for high-performance distributed chassis.

papers.title: Autonomous Scanning Electrochemical Cell Microscopy Enables Rapid Exploration of Large Compositionally Complex Material Spaces
papers.abstract: Alloying is a central strategy in electrocatalysis, enabling fine‐tuning of the electronic structure. In particular, compositionally complex solid solutions (CCSSs), often called high‐entropy alloys, are of high interest. However, the “combinatorial explosion” in the number of possible compositions poses a critical bottleneck for the discovery of CCSS electrocatalysts. We present an autonomous scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM) system for ultrahigh‐throughput and large‐scale CCSS activity screening. The platform rapidly establishes composition–activity relationships across multiple thin‐film CCSS materials libraries via active learning and automated library exchange. Embedding analytical expressions of voltammetry in the algorithm enables the learning of whole voltammograms rather than a single selected metric. As a demonstration, we investigated hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) activities of Au–Ir–Rh, where Ir and Rh exhibit strong metal‐hydrogen binding and Au exhibits weak binding as derived from the HER volcano plot. The activity trend was accurately predicted after measuring only 15% of all 966 measurement areas. Au 30 Ir 20 Rh 50 and Au 10 Ir 35 Rh 55 exhibit the highest activities with standard rate constants of ∼0.012 cm s −1 , demonstrating positive synergistic contributions from elemental mixing. The proposed platform is broadly applicable to a wide range of electrocatalytic reactions, providing a general pathway for accelerating CCSS electrocatalyst discovery.

papers.title: Coaxially Printed Electroactive Mineralized Devices Multimodally Release Immunotherapeutic Molecules for Personalized Postoperative Treatment of Heterogeneous Bone Tumors
papers.abstract: Regenerative devices that modulate the in vivo release doses of immunoregulatory therapeutic molecules based on the action mechanisms of signaling pathways and individual responses play a key role in the postoperative treatment of heterogeneous malignant bone tumors. Herein, a core–shell‐structured electroactive mineralized device capable of multimodally regulating the local macrophage phenotype and phagocytic behavior on demand was fabricated by coaxial‐printing using a cellulose nanocrystal (CNC)/calcium phosphate‐based inner‐flow bioink loaded with the CD47/signal regulatory protein‐α pathway inhibitor RRX‐001 and the osteogenic compensator icariin (IC) together with a polysaccharide‐based outer‐flow bioink crosslinked with the CSF‐1R inhibitor GW2580. GW2580 was incorporated into the shell through dynamic covalent bonds and electrostatic interactions, thereby enabling relatively rapid release and efficiently reducing M2 polarization of local macrophages. Incorporation of the piezoelectric component CNC into the device core enabled the controlled release of RRX‐001 upon wireless ultrasonic force triggering, regulating macrophage phagocytic function through the proton motive force‐driven mitochondrial ATP synthesis pathway based on individual responses. Simultaneously, the released IC counteracted the side effects induced by immune regulation and facilitated bone regeneration. In summary, core–shell‐structured electroactive mineralized devices that enable multimodal regulation of macrophage functions offer a personalized therapeutic strategy for the postoperative treatment of bone tumors.

papers.title: An integrated lightweight vision-control framework for UAV-to-UAV following
papers.abstract: Onboard UAV-to-UAV following is challenged by small target size, tracker drift, occlusion, and limited computing resources. This paper presents a lightweight vision–control framework for fixed-altitude UAV-to-UAV following, combining center-only LightFC, hybrid-triggered persistent re-detection, YOLO26-DC, and PN-guided enumerative model predictive control (E-MPC). Center-only LightFC performs high-frequency center localization, while YOLO26 conducts continuous global search at startup and after either P-trigger or Q-trigger activation until a valid detection updates the target center, scale, and template. YOLO26-DC integrates DySample and context anchor attention to improve small-UAV detection and supports TensorRT deployment. Center-only LightFC reduces GFLOPs by 27.8% relative to LightFC and achieves an online tracking throughput of 106.7 FPS with TensorRT on Jetson. The hybrid-trigger strategy obtains a MeanCE of 8.65 and an F-score of 0.84 on DUT Anti-UAV Tracking. YOLO26-DC reaches 0.911 mAP50 and 0.542 mAP50-95 with only 0.022 M additional parameters and 0.19 GFLOPs compared with baseline YOLO26. In the evaluated low-speed Gazebo table occlusion scenarios, compared with PN-guided MPPI, PN-guided E-MPC reduces the mean tracking error outside the table area by 48.0% and the control energy by 68.4%. Indoor flight tests demonstrate closed-loop execution and recovery from short-term target loss.

papers.title: Redefining Value in Total Joint Arthroplasty Reproducibility as the Primary Currency in the Era of Robotics
papers.abstract: The debate surrounding robotics in total joint arthroplasty (TJA) has largely centered on acquisition costs, operative efficiency, technical precision, and early clinical outcomes.1,2 Although these considerations are essential, conventional assessments of value predominantly emphasize mean patient-reported outcomes, complication rates, implant survivorship, and episode-ofcare expenditures.Such measures provide important benchmarks for clinical effectiveness but may not fully characterize the consistency with which favorable outcomes are achieved across patients, surgeons, and healthcare institutions.Modern TJA represents a complex system of care in which surgical technique, patient characteristics, implant selection, and perioperative management collectively influence outcomes.Consequently, evaluating performance requires consideration not only of average clinical results but also of their distribution, predictability, and reproducibility.Principles derived from high-reliability industries suggest that reducing unwarranted variation may contribute to more consistent system performance.3 However, unlike standardized industrial processes, arthroplasty involves biological variability and individualized clinical decision-making, making the elimination of variation neither feasible nor necessarily desirable.Importantly, technical reproducibility, defined as the consistent achievement of intended surgical targets, must be distinguished from clinical reproducibility, defined as the consistent achievement of meaningful patient outcomes.Although robotic technologies may improve the precision and consistency of surgical execution, evidence that these improvements reliably translate into superior functional outcomes, reduced complications, improved implant survivorship, or lower healthcare expenditures remains inconclusive.We therefore propose that reproducibility be examined as an additional, potentially important dimension of value in TJA, rather than as an established surrogate for clinical effectiveness.The objective of this perspective is to examine reproducibility as a complementary dimension of arthroplasty value, critically distinguish technical precision from demonstrated clinical benefit, and propose measurable domains for future clinical and economic evaluation. The limitations of mean-based value metricsTraditional assessments of value in TJA emphasize aggregate measures, including mean improvements in patient-reported outcomes, complication rates, revision-free survivorship, and episode-of-care costs.4 Although these metrics are indispensable, measures of central tendency alone may obscure clinically meaningful differences in outcome distributions.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Cascade Neural Network for Reliable Prediction of CO2/H2O Co-Electrolysis in SOEC
papers.abstract: Co-electrolysis of CO 2 /H 2 O in solid oxide electrochemical cell (SOEC) is an emerging technology for renewable hydrogen and synthetic fuels. This study proposes a Physics-Informed Cascade Neural Network (PCNN) for reliable multi-objective performance prediction. PCNN integrates a cascade propagation mechanism to capture causal relationships among variables, an adaptive weighting strategy using homoscedastic uncertainty for multi-objective optimization, and a physics-informed grey-box architecture to identify hidden non-ideal parameters. Trained on published SOEC data and validated with independent experiments, PCNN consistently outperforms conventional artificial neural network (ANN), convolutional neural network (CNN), cascade-forward neural network (CFNN), and physics-informed neural network (PINN) models, achieving over 99% prediction accuracy. It also estimates Faradaic efficiency and non-ideal heat loss, improving interpretability and reducing the mean relative residual of mass conservation from 9.02% to 3.21%. This framework offers a general methodology for intelligent modeling and control of SOEC co-electrolysis and other electrochemical energy conversion systems.

papers.title: Operating-regime dependence of turbulence effects on an H-type Darrieus vertical-axis wind turbine using uncertainty-aware surrogate modeling
papers.abstract: The aerodynamic response of an H-type Darrieus vertical-axis wind turbine to inflow turbulence depends on the rotor operating regime and cannot be represented by a single turbulence correction. This study examines the coupled effects of free-stream velocity, tip speed ratio, and turbulence intensity for a fixed-geometry, three-bladed rotor using an 85-case two-dimensional unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes database. The retained cases span free-stream velocities of 6, 9, and 12 m/s, tip speed ratios of 1.5–3.5, and turbulence intensities of 1%–25%. Gaussian process regression, random forest, and extreme gradient boosting are used as surrogate tools to interpolate the computed operating map and are evaluated using nested five-fold cross-validation. Across the sampled conditions, the highest power coefficient occurs at a tip speed ratio of 2.5. Increasing turbulence from 1% to 25% reduces the peak power coefficient by approximately 3%–6%, whereas the reduction reaches 17% at a tip speed ratio of 1.5 and 9 m/s. A local non-monotonic response also appears near a tip speed ratio of 2.0 and turbulence intensities of 10%–15%. SHapley Additive exPlanations identify tip speed ratio as the dominant input, while turbulence intensity has a smaller global contribution but a strongly operating-regime-dependent effect. The three nonlinear surrogates are statistically comparable; Gaussian process regression gives a root-mean-square error of 0.0047 and provides predictive variance for interpolation within the sampled domain. The results show that the surrogate is most useful as an uncertainty-aware representation of operating-condition interactions within the adopted two-dimensional numerical framework.

papers.title: It Is Not the Twin that Speaks: Digital Triplets and the Emergence of Voice Between Them
papers.abstract: Digital twins built from biographical archives can generate responses that sound like historical individuals and are grounded in their writings. Yet a source-grounded utterance is not the same as something the person actually said. This distinction raises fundamental questions about voice, interpretation, and responsibility in life-writing research. This article explores these questions through an experiment with a digital twin of the Norwegian-Danish author Amalie Skram (1846–1905). The starting point was an unfinished manuscript fragment that appears to open a fifth volume of her novel series Hellemyrsfolket. Asked to explore how the story might have continued, the twin produced coherent responses but tended to explain the fragment through patterns already established in Skram's writing, thereby reducing its ambiguity. To investigate this limitation, I developed a configuration of three separate, source-grounded models: Skram's own writings, contemporary accounts, and later scholarship. I call this the digital triplets. Rather than reconstructing an authoritative historical voice, the method keeps different perspectives in productive tension. What emerges is not the recovered voice of the historical subject, but a new interpretive relation for which the researcher remains responsible.

papers.title: Mechanics-Informed Machine Learning Using Classical Lamination Theory-Derived Data for Screening and Ranking Carbon/Basalt/Glass Hybrid Laminates
papers.abstract: Hybrid composite laminates provide broad design flexibility, but their mechanical response depends on coupled effects of ply material, stacking sequence, ply number, ply position, and fiber volume fraction. This study presents a mechanics-informed machine learning framework for the preliminary screening and ranking of symmetric carbon/basalt/glass epoxy hybrid laminates. Symmetric 4-, 6-, and 8-ply configurations were generated using unidirectional carbon, basalt, and glass plies. Classical Lamination Theory was used to calculate tensile modulus, flexural modulus, a lamina-level longitudinal tensile strength indicator, nominal first-failure stress, and tensile resilience at selected fiber volume fractions. The resulting analytical dataset was used to train Support Vector Regression, Multi-Layer Perceptron, and Gaussian Process Regression models after Bayesian hyperparameter optimization. On the held-out analytical test set, Gaussian Process Regression reproduced the CLT-derived targets most closely, with an overall R² of 0.991. The trained model was then used for laminate ranking, feature-importance analysis, and Monte Carlo-based design-space exploration. Carbon-rich laminates showed the highest overall performance, while selected carbon–glass hybrids offered competitive balanced responses. The framework provides a physically interpretable tool for screening hybrid laminate designs before experimental validation.

papers.title: Short-form videos for digital science communication A multimodal analysis of STEM university students' practices
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of digital technologies has transformed the pedagogical demands placed on university lecturers regarding digital and multimodal literacy and (science) communication skills. A popular form of communicating science online refers to short-form videos, such as Science Crowdfunding Videos (SCVs) (Vivas-Peraza, 2026) or 60-second science videos, which combine oral, visual, and gestural semiotic resources to address specialist and non-specialist audiences (Kress & van Leeuwen 2020; Luzón 2019). Integrating the teaching of such digital genres into university courses fosters the development of students’ multimodal composing competencies and digital literacy skills (Belcher 2017). Yet research on the strategies deployed by students when crafting short-form science videos remains scarce, particularly within ESP (English for Specific Purposes)/EMI (English-Medium Instruction) settings. For instance, Lai et al. (2025) highlight the need for evidence-based training for audiovisual science communication practices in pedagogical contexts. As a result, this paper aims to identify students’ multimodal composing strategies and communication strategies when creating short-form science videos and to propose pedagogical guidelines that contribute to the teaching of digital science communication. This paper reports on an exploratory interdisciplinary study conducted with students enrolled in the English-taught Biophysics Master’s Programme during the 2025-26 academic year. Students were asked to produce short-form science dissemination videos in English after an introductory session on digital genres’ principles and multimodal strategies. Drawing on multimodal discourse analysis (Belcher 2017; Jewitt 2013; Kress & van Leeuwen 2020) and digital genre-based pedagogy (Hafner 2020), a dataset of student-produced videos (n=6) was analysed using Atlas.ti software to identify patterns in the use of oral, visual, and kinesics resources (e.g., body language, gestures). The qualitative content analysis was complemented with student pre- and post-task surveys, as well as teacher assessment based on the CEFR and the CFRIDiL frameworks. Preliminary findings reveal enhanced scientific communication for non-specialist audiences through the strategic deployment of multimodal resources (i.e., images, voice, editing and body language). That is, students demonstrate strength in content organisation and multimodal composition. Furthermore, the digital nature of the task also increases student motivation and active learning through the creative production of audiovisual content. These findings are expected to contribute to digital genre pedagogy and the development of digital skills in higher education, offering insights regarding the collaboration between ESP/EMI lecturers. This collaboration can equip future scientists with the digital multimodal literacy skills demanded by today’s science communication demands. METHODS: This study proposes a novel ultrasound-guided model predictive control method for needle steering. It incorporates a mechanics-based model that accounts for muscle anisotropy and tissue heterogeneity, integrated with ultrasound-based trajectory reconstruction to predict needle deflection. The control strategy is designed to minimise insertion error, the number of rotations, and rotation depth. RESULTS: mm error) for given tasks while minimising tissue trauma. CONCLUSIONS: The proposed method significantly enhances the insertion accuracy and reduces tissue damage, as indicated by the reduced number and depth of needle rotations, for robot-assisted percutaneous in anisotropic, heterogeneous tissue. These results provide a validated foundation for future clinical translation of the proposed control framework.

papers.title: 1353-UR Uncertainty Quantification in Bayesian Neural Networks for Image-Based Concentration Prediction
papers.abstract: This study investigated whether a Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) could predict antigen concentrations from images and estimate predictive uncertainty under Gaussian image noise. A LeNet-5-inspired BNN was trained using 298 images from five concentration groups. Four noise settings (0, 1, 5, and 50) were evaluated using five-fold training/validation splits and a fixed test set. Prediction accuracy was measured with mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE), while uncertainty was estimated from 15 stochastic predictions per image. Results showed substantial prediction errors and variation across folds. The highest noise setting had the lowest average error and uncertainty, but the effects of noise were not consistent.

papers.title: What Must a Model Tell a Planner? Outcome Interfaces for Risk-Aware Planning After Robot Damage
papers.abstract: When a robot is damaged, it must decide which routes it can still afford, and the amount of risk it may accept can change from one mission to the next. We argue that whether a learned model helps such a robot depends on its decision interface, that is, on what the model hands to the planner. A decision policy tells the planner what to do, whereas an outcome model, a kind of world model, predicts the consequences of each route. We study simulated Unitree Go2 quadrupeds and H1 humanoids with weakened motors, added payloads, or reduced foot friction. We compare four interfaces. The first is a decision policy, and the second is the same policy trained with fixed penalties for infeasible routes. The third is an outcome model that predicts the feasibility and travel time of each route. The fourth, which we call a capability contract, is an outcome model that predicts the chance of success and the travel time of the robot on each terrain and composes them along a route. All share the same collected experience, matched tuning and risk calibration, and an uncertainty guard. Two comparatively low-risk probes let the capability contract rank hazardous terrains about as well as four new trials on every hazard. At a calibrated 5% limit on selecting empirically infeasible routes, outcome models cut declined missions from about 32% to 7-8% on Go2 and from 57% to 35-36% on H1 compared with the plain policy. Fixed penalties narrow this gap, but the best penalty changes with the risk target. Predicting outcomes lets the planner preserve missions by changing routes as risk requirements tighten.

papers.title: Augmentation of cardiovascular flow measurements with generative diffusion models
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular imaging offers several ways to measure blood flow, but each provides an incomplete, resolution-limited, or noisy view of the underlying dynamics. Reconstructing the missing information is inherently ambiguous because several flow fields may be compatible with the same observation. Here, we investigate generative diffusion models as tools for cardiovascular-flow generation and reconstruction using a fully controlled state-of-the-art dataset from a digital twin of a healthy human left heart. First, we show how unconditional samples reproduce the changing anatomy and the highly fluctuating statistical properties of the flow throughout the cardiac cycle. Second, we test the conditional inference of our generative model by reconstructing an entire 2D planar section of geometry and flow configurations from a limited portion. Repeated reconstructions allow us to represent a range of plausible completions, going beyond a single deterministic estimate, while their mean retains the principal features of the reference flow. Comparison with a Gaussian process regression baseline on the same reduced domain highlights the main advantage of diffusion models: their reconstructed ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations, better encompassing ground-truth features that the baseline distributions can miss. Our results provide a quantitative proof of concept for probabilistic reconstruction of incomplete cardiovascular-flow measurements and demonstrate the potential for groundbreaking applications to the augmentation of in-vivo cardiovascular imaging data.

papers.title: Budgeted Subset Selection with a Transferable Learned Value Model
papers.abstract: Subset selection is a fundamental task in machine learning, statistics and combinatorial optimisation, with applications in active learning, band selection, input selection and experimental design. The utility of a subset depends on information revealed only after the selection, such as labels or responses, and on interactions among selected candidates. Existing approaches combine value estimation and redundancy control in application-specific ways, which limits their use in other domains. This paper introduces Subset Acquisition with Learned Value Estimates and Search (SALVES), a framework that decomposes subset selection into two components. First, a value model is trained by supervised learning on tasks where the hidden information is known. On a new task, it predicts the utility each candidate would add to the current selection. Second, a selection step chooses the subset from these predictions, typically by simulated annealing with a diversity term penalising redundancy. The value model transfers to new classes, pretrained networks, datasets and sensors, and from synthetic to real data. On the four applications, SALVES matches or outperforms application-specific baselines on average. It requires substantially fewer bands for equal accuracy and remains reliable in input selection where individual baselines fail.

papers.title: Trust What Repeats: Capped World-Model Policy Gradients for Humanoid Motion Tracking
papers.abstract: Training a humanoid motion tracker by backpropagating imagined returns through a learned world model is fast, because the model gives a first-order policy gradient. We ask how much of that gradient holds in the simulator. On a tracker for the Unitree G1, the $0.5\%$ of imagined rollouts with the largest gradients carry $22\%$ of the summed gradient norm, yet neither a second rollout from the same state nor the simulator confirms them. When the actions are moved along the model's gradient, the simulator returns 94% of the predicted change in return where the gradient norm is below the batch median, 48% between 3 and 10 times the median, and 1% above 30 times; the part of a gradient that either check confirms stops growing at a few times the median. We therefore cap each rollout's action-gradient norm at 10 times the batch median, draw imagination starts in proportion to their predicted gradient norm so that the cap removes less, and reset episodes where the world model and critic predict the lowest return. Trained on 223 hours of motion and tested on 353 motions that no actor performed in training, the method raises the normalized return of SuperMimic, the baseline it builds on, from 0.953 to 0.967 and the lowest $1\%$ of test clips from 0.65 to 0.76, halves the test clips that fall persistently, from 15--18 to 7--10, and reaches the baseline's final return in 40% of the baseline's iterations and half its training time. On LAFAN1, trained and evaluated on the same clips as prior work, it reaches 0.935 against 0.906.

papers.title: Efficient VLA Reinforcement Learning via Subchunk Rollouts in Latent World Models
papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) can improve pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies through imagined experiences. However, existing VLA-MBRL methods primarily rely on large-scale image or video generation world models, incurring large computational overhead. Latent world models offer a more efficient alternative but face two challenges: compounding errors during recursive prediction and incompatibility with VLAs' visual input interfaces. In this work, we propose LS-MBPO, a lightweight residual MBRL framework that leverages latent world models to improve upon pretrained VLAs. LS-MBPO introduces two key techniques: (1) Hierarchical Forcing, which combines dense causal supervision with autoregressive feedback to mitigate compounding prediction errors; and (2) Latent Subchunk Rollouts, which leverage action chunks from a frozen VLA policy and a latent residual policy for successive subchunk refinement, bridging the gap between latent imagination and VLA policy execution. We further introduce a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum that progressively shifts rollout starting points from later to earlier task stages, enabling effective policy learning from short imagined rollouts. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot show that LS-MBPO achieves superior task performance and training efficiency compared to existing methods.

papers.title: SOAR: Training-Free Rank-Consistent Rollout Compression for Latent World Model Planning
papers.abstract: Latent world models plan by rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences through a transformer predictor, so a single decision can take tens of seconds. Existing accelerations prune spatial tokens as in vision-language models, yet a sampling-based planner uses predicted costs only to rank candidates, so a rollout can be compressed freely as long as the ranking survives. We propose SOAR, a training-free method that adapts rollout compression to each planning decision. At every decision, SOAR probes a few candidates under several token budgets and keeps the smallest budget that preserves their ranking, so it compresses as far as the current decision allows, without task labels. A closed-loop study of more than 80,000 episodes fixes the rest of the rollout: the first step, which alone reads a real observation, stays exact, and the context frame is cached rather than recomputed. On seven navigation and manipulation tasks with frozen checkpoints, SOAR matches dense-level planning success at 2.3x speedup and retains 98% at 2.5x. Our code is available at https://github.com/starrywiki/SOAR.

papers.title: Do DeepONet Trunk-Basis Preconditioners Need Training?
papers.abstract: Trunk-basis (TB) preconditioners build the coarse space of a two-level Schwarz preconditioner from the trunk functions of a trained deep operator network (DeepONet), restricted to subdomains. Their effectiveness has been attributed to spectral bias since networks learn low frequencies first, complementing a smoother that removes the high-frequency error. Spectral bias, however, is a property of training, whereas a randomly initialized trunk with a smooth activation is already smooth. We therefore ask whether TB preconditioners need training. In one dimension, we prove that on each subdomain the span of untrained trunk functions is close to the space of low-degree polynomials under suitable nondegeneracy assumptions. Numerically, for the Poisson equation and three-dimensional linear elasticity with constant coefficients, untrained TB and piecewise polynomial coarse spaces of equal dimension yield close conjugate gradient iteration counts, while training with the standard \(\ell^2\) loss sometimes increases them. Training can improve iteration counts when high-contrast coefficients make the low-energy modes non-smooth, and if the loss measures the error in the energy norm. For the Poisson equation with contrast \(10^5\), energy-trained TB coarse spaces need fewer iterations than piecewise polynomials of equal dimension, whereas \(\ell^2\)-trained ones do not. For a topology-optimized elastic cantilever with contrast \(10^6\), the energy-trained TB space enriched with the rigid-body modes gives the fewest iterations at larger coarse dimensions. This suggests that for neural operator-based hybrid solvers, a network's inductive bias and training objective should match the solver.

The learning factory consists of an AGV, three robots, two conveyors and their digital twins. Three typical use cases are designed to demonstrate the capabilities of the learning factory, i.e., material sorting through computer vision-based robot control, coordinating AGV, robots and conveyors for assembly, and digital twin-driven predictive maintenance. The results show that the developed learning factory can adequately support the teaching and research activities on digital twins and AI on manufacturing. Its fully open-source architecture and relatively low deployment cost make it an ideal solution for universities and research institutions.

papers.title: PhiJEPA: Denoising Latent Predictions for Visual Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Can a predictor trained to infer hidden image regions still help a world model plan when part of an object disappears from view and the visible context is blurred? We introduce PhiJEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that adapts PhiNet's two-stage prediction to masked Transformers. From sparse, photometrically corrupted context, a Transformer block predicts hidden tokens of an independently corrupted teacher view. A token-wise MLP then maps these predictions to clean teacher tokens. Controlled ablations show that the combined objective improves dense features over the tested one-stage alternatives. Pre-trained on ImageNet-1K with $5.6\times10^{19}$ training FLOPs, PhiJEPA achieves 69.3 mIoU on linear PASCAL VOC segmentation, exceeding the evaluated I-JEPA and DSeq-JEPA checkpoints in segmentation accuracy, with 25\% fewer training FLOPs than I-JEPA. It also improves hidden-region segmentation over Simple I-JEPA (49.1 vs.\ 44.3 mIoU). As an application, we use the frozen encoder in DINO-WM on PushT, and reuse the pre-training predictor, which JEPAs usually discard, to complete occluded tokens without fine-tuning. In open-loop planning with simultaneous object occlusion and Gaussian blur ($σ=2$ pixels), predictor completion raises success from 33\% to 65\%, compared with 25\% for Simple I-JEPA with its predictor and 40\% for iBOT with pixel inpainting. Together, these results support two-stage latent prediction as an efficient approach to learning visual representations that remain useful under photometric degradation and support completion under partial observation.

papers.title: Ego4Gen: Generating Geometry-Grounded Motion Tokens as a World-Action Interface
papers.abstract: We present Ego4Gen (Egocentric 4D Future Generation), a world model for 4D future generation in robotic manipu lation. Given a single egocentric image and a text prompt, Ego4Gen jointly generates temporally aligned RGB frames, dense point maps, and dense scene flow, explicitly pre dicting the evolution of scene appearance, spatial struc ture, and motion. Built on Cosmos3-Nano, Ego4Gen ex tends the pretrained generative backbone through modality routed LoRA and asymmetric attention, using geometric pseudo-labels from MotionCrafter to learn to predict future geometry and motion latents. These latents can either be decoded into explicit 3D structure and motion or mapped to robot actions. To this end, we also introduce FlowIn verse, a lightweight inverse dynamics network trained in two stages to translate predicted 4D latents into robot ac tions. Experiments show that these geometry and motion latents outperform the evaluated latent-action and video latent baselines in out-of-distribution settings. Closed loop policy evaluations further demonstrate their utility for translating predicted 4D futures into robot control. To gether, these results support geometry-grounded motion to kens as a world-action interface, connecting 4D future gen eration with robotic manipulation and suggesting a path to ward reduced reliance on action-labeled data.

papers.title: Learned Network Dynamics for Model Predictive Traffic Signal Control under Incidents
papers.abstract: Model predictive control (MPC) of urban traffic signals relies on a model of how queues respond to signal decisions, which is hard to specify and calibrate in heterogeneous networks, particularly when incidents change capacities and turning shares. Measurements add a second limitation: the controlled lanes at the stop line are often short, so queues extending upstream of them fall outside lane-level measurements. We propose GNN-MPC, a receding-horizon controller that plans with action-conditioned network dynamics learned by graph neural networks. Phase sequences are coordinated across intersections by approximate best responses, with an acceptance test that keeps the predicted cost no higher than that of the initial plan. In microscopic simulation under non-recurrent incidents, GNN-MPC reduces travel time and increases completed trips relative to all tested controllers, on a homogeneous grid and a heterogeneous 21-intersection network. Controlled comparisons on the heterogeneous network distinguish the roles of observation and prediction. With nearly as many vehicles entering the network, GNN-MPC reduces travel time by 13% relative to MaxPressure with the same upstream measurement, and GNN-MPC without the upstream representation does not reproduce its performance. Under the same traffic measurements, planner and objective, replacing the learned dynamics with calibrated store-and-forward predictors increases travel time by 31-34%. Observing hidden demand and predicting its response to control are thus complementary requirements of network-level predictive control.
